title: NEXUS-GO
points: Good morning, and thank you for being here; this is my Master's defense at the Institute of Computing of Unicamp.
I was supervised by Professor Zanoni Dias, with Professor Hélio Pedrini and Doctor Gabriel Bianchin de Oliveira as co-advisors.
The question: how far can a protein interaction network go toward predicting function, alone and with a protein language model?
My answer is NEXUS-GO, which propagates ProtT5 embeddings over the STRING interaction network.
transition: Let me show how the talk is organized.

title: Roadmap
points: The talk has six parts: motivation, background, data and evaluation, method, results and conclusions.
The method is presented as two generations of models and four NEXUS-GO routes.
The results cover ablations, the literature comparison, cost and the role of connectivity.
Every model is described by three decisions: representation, propagation and prediction head.
transition: Let me start with the motivation.

title: Millions of sequences, few known functions
points: Proteins take part in almost every process in a living cell.
Sequencing is fast, but characterizing a function in the laboratory is slow and expensive.
So databases fill with sequences much faster than with experimental annotations; the bars are not to scale.
CAFA, the Critical Assessment of Functional Annotation, scores predictors on proteins whose function was not yet public.
transition: To predict a function, we first need a way to write it down.

title: Function as a hierarchy of terms
points: The Gene Ontology has three parts, always shown in this order: BP, CC and MF.
Each ontology is a directed acyclic graph of terms, linked by relations such as is_a and part_of.
The True Path Rule says a protein with a term also has every ancestor of that term, up to the root.
Every model's predictions are made consistent before any metric; the task is hierarchical multi-label classification.
transition: The sequence, however, is not the whole story.

title: Function also depends on context
points: Proteins rarely act alone; they form complexes and take part in pathways.
We model these relations as a PPI network: proteins are nodes, associations are edges.
Guilt by association: connected proteins tend to share functions, a probabilistic guideline, not a rule.
STRING mixes evidence of uneven reliability, and about one third of our proteins have no edge at all.
transition: This leads to seven research questions.

title: Seven research questions
points: The first three ask about representation and architecture: network representation, the gain from propagating ProtT5, fixed versus learned aggregation.
The next two ask whether early and late fusion help, and how deep propagation should go with how much retention.
The last two compare with the literature and test one global network pooling all species and evidence channels.
I will answer each question at the end.
transition: Here is what the work contributes.

title: Contributions
points: First, NEXUS-GO: a non-parametric, multi-hop propagation of ProtT5 embeddings over STRING.
Second, fixed propagation against learned aggregation with GCN and GAT; third, a vector head against an image head.
Fourth, early and late fusion; fifth, a benchmark against five methods retrained on the same splits.
The work produced a VISAPP 2026 paper and an extended version accepted in CCIS, expected in December 2026.
transition: Now the background, starting with graphs.

title: Graphs, adjacency and message passing
points: A graph is a set of nodes and edges, here proteins and associations weighted by STRING confidence.
Protein networks are very sparse, so memory grows with the number of edges, not proteins squared.
Graph neural networks pass messages: each node aggregates its neighbours and updates itself.
L layers see an L-hop neighbourhood, but too many layers cause oversmoothing.
transition: Three more building blocks appear later in the talk.

title: Building blocks
points: The multilayer perceptron, or MLP, is the vector prediction head of my models.
The convolutional network slides small filters over an image; I use ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-Tiny in the image route.
The autoencoder compresses its input and reconstructs it; deepNF uses it on its diffusion states.
transition: The other ingredient is the protein language model.

title: Protein language models
points: Protein language models learn by self-supervision on hundreds of millions of sequences, with no labels.
A transformer encoder reads each residue in the context of the whole protein.
I use ProtT5-XL-U50, pretrained on BFD and UniRef50 with 15% masking, and read layers 22, 23 and 24.
Each layer is averaged over residues and joined; the model stays frozen, giving a fixed-length vector.
transition: Let me place this work in the literature.

title: From neighbour voting to graph transformers
points: The field moved from neighbour voting to diffusion, node embeddings, graph neural networks and graph transformers.
Each step added parameters, tuning surface and cost.
I retrained five methods: Mashup, deepNF, MELISSA, DeepGraphGO and SEGT-GO.
My position: a frozen language model, a fixed multi-hop diffusion, and only an MLP head is trained.
transition: This review leaves an open question.

title: The open question
points: Is a learned graph component still needed once the propagated object is already informative?
I propagate ProtT5 embeddings with a fixed operator for a finite number of steps, then use an ordinary head.
The contribution is an architectural placement, not a new propagation mechanism.
A sequence representation exists for every protein, so the network only adds to it.
transition: Part three: the data and the evaluation.

title: Data: a CAFA5-derived corpus
points: The corpus comes from the CAFA5 training data; in BP there are 73,768 training proteins and 9,221 each for validation and test.
Each ontology keeps its most frequent terms: 500 in BP, 498 in CC and 499 in MF.
The split is 80, 10 and 10 percent at the protein level, so every comparison is internal.
Labels are sparse: 25.91 terms on average in BP, and only 5.18% positive entries in BP.
transition: The network is STRING, version 11.5.

title: STRING v11.5: one aggregated network
points: The file has 2,422,234 records but only 791,011 distinct pairs over 86,423 proteins.
Combined scores range from 0.400 to 0.999 and express confidence, not binding strength.
Each pair appears 3.06 times on average with the same score, so repetitions add no information.
Degrees are heavy-tailed: the median protein has 5 to 7 neighbours, the largest hubs 763 to 805.
transition: Now the most important property of this network.

title: One third of the proteins have no edge
points: About one third of the proteins have no edge: 36.65% in BP, 34.95% in CC and 32.19% in MF.
The fraction is stable across training, validation and test, and isolated proteins stay as nodes.
A higher confidence threshold only makes it worse; at 0.90 more than half are isolated.
For a network-only model, a third of the corpus has no input, which the second generation removes.
transition: How are the predictions scored?

title: Six protein-centric metrics
points: The primary criterion is wF_max, the F-measure weighted by information content, used to select every configuration.
I also report F_max, its variant without the root, S_min in bits, and two areas under the precision-recall curve.
Predictions are made hierarchy-consistent before scoring.
The threshold sweeps 101 values, and a protein with no prediction counts as zero recall.
transition: The last part of the setup is the learning protocol.

title: Learning regime and protocol
points: The setting is transductive: one graph, but the loss reads only training labels.
Every design decision is taken on validation; the test set is read once, at the end.
All runs use a single seed, so differences below 0.5 pp are ties, my interpretability floor.
transition: Part four: the method.

title: Two generations, three decisions
points: Every model is defined by three decisions: representation, propagation and prediction head.
The first generation uses the network alone: a protein's row of the STRING matrix, with an MLP or CNN head.
About one third of proteins are isolated, so for them that representation is a null vector.
The second generation, NEXUS-GO, starts from ProtT5 and propagates it, fixed or with a GCN or GAT.
transition: Let me first describe the first generation.

title: Generation 1: the network alone
points: The input is the protein's row of the weighted adjacency matrix, restricted to training proteins.
I keep the profile raw or reduce it with maximum or average pooling.
The vector route uses an MLP or a one-dimensional CNN.
The image route turns 224 pooled values into a 224 by 224 image for ResNet-50 or ConvNeXt-Tiny.
transition: Here is the wall this generation hits.

title: An isolated protein has no input
points: For an isolated protein the profile is all zeros, so the image is uniform.
The head can only return the learned class prior, the same answer for every isolated protein.
No architecture can recover information absent from the input.
The next generation needs a representation for every protein, and the sequence gives one.
transition: This is NEXUS-GO at a glance.

title: NEXUS-GO: four routes
points: The frozen ProtT5 encoder turns each sequence into H(0), a 3,072-dimensional vector that exists for every protein.
STRING records are deduplicated with the maximum rule into W, and column normalization gives P.
NEXUS-GO/Fixed propagates H(0) with P without parameters; NEXUS-GO/GNN learns the aggregation with a GCN or GAT.
NEXUS-GO/Early joins the two representations; NEXUS-GO/Late combines their probabilities with a linear rule.
transition: Let me open each block, starting with the sequence representation.

title: ProtT5-XL-U50, three layers, frozen
points: ProtT5 reads at most 1,022 tokens, so long sequences are chunked and averaged.
Layers 24, 23 and 22 give 1,024 dimensions each, 3,072 when concatenated.
Three adjacent layers avoid betting on a single layer and add nothing to tune.
This representation exists for every protein; the pipeline is inherited from SUPERMAGOv2.
transition: Next, the graph.

title: From records to an operator
points: W is symmetric, without self-loops, stored sparse with at most 1,133,132 entries instead of 25 to 35 GB dense.
Summation rewards how often a pair was written: A at 0.80 five times gets 4.00 against B at 0.95.
The maximum keeps the STRING score on its own scale, so B comes first; that is my rule.
Normalizing each column gives P, so a neighbour's weight is relative to the protein's other neighbours.
transition: Now the core of the method: fixed propagation.

title: Fixed propagation: no parameters
points: Each step keeps a fraction α of the previous representation and takes one minus α from the weighted neighbours, repeated T times.
Nothing is trained, so the result is computed once, cached and reused at every epoch.
Many steps cause oversmoothing, and isolated nodes only shrink toward grey; a higher α changes much less.
T equal to 0 or α equal to 1 switches the graph off: that is the ProtT5 baseline.
transition: What does this do to real proteins?

title: Propagation on four real proteins
points: Four Cellular Component proteins, from a hub of degree 798 to an isolated protein, before and after six steps with α at 0.4.
The connected proteins keep their structure while absorbing their neighbourhood.
The isolated protein is only scaled by α to the power T, so its image fades to grey.
Changes on degree-zero proteins reflect this rescaling and head retraining, not neighbourhood information.
transition: The alternative is to learn the aggregation.

title: Learned propagation: GCN and GAT
points: The GCN adds self-loops, normalizes symmetrically and takes the STRING confidence as given.
The GAT learns attention over neighbours with four heads, re-estimating how much each one counts.
Both have two layers of width 1,024 and output a 1,024-dimensional embedding, g.
A learned operator must re-propagate the whole graph, about 289 times per epoch, while the fixed route does it once.
transition: Two prediction heads consume these representations.

title: Vector head and vision head
points: The vector head is an MLP with hidden layers of 1,024 and 512 units and a dropout of 0.4.
The vision head turns the 3,072 values into three 32 by 32 channels, one per ProtT5 layer.
The backbones are ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-Tiny, pretrained on ImageNet and fully fine-tuned.
Caution: pixel adjacency here only reflects storage order, and the results show that this matters.
transition: Every model is trained with the same objective.

title: Training objective: ProteinLoss
points: ProteinLoss is a product of three factors: ZLPR and two factors of one minus a weighted F1.
ZLPR separates a protein's positive terms from its negative ones around zero.
The two soft F1 factors are weighted by information content, one per term column and one per protein row.
In the first generation it beats binary cross-entropy by 5.47 pp on the mean, so every later run uses it.
transition: The last piece of the method is fusion.

title: Combining the fixed and learned routes
points: The fixed and learned routes use the confidence differently, so I combine them instead of choosing.
Early fusion trains one head on joined representations, of 4,096 or 3,072 dimensions.
Late fusion trains each route alone and combines probabilities afterwards, with no further training.
I compare eleven late rules, choosing coefficients on validation over 71 configurations per ontology.
transition: Part five: the results.

title: 170 runs, one funnel
points: The campaign has 170 runs and about 136.3 GPU-hours, 147 of them on an RTX A5500.
Selection is a funnel: each stage passes only its validation winner to the next.
Two stations are not pure validation picks: the maximum rule, and ConvNeXt-Tiny on a 0.57 pp margin.
The test set is read once, at the end, for the frozen winner, NEXUS-GO/Late.
transition: First, what the network alone can do.

title: Generation 1 settles three choices
points: A naive baseline that looks at nothing reaches a mean wF_max of 43.56.
ProteinLoss beats binary cross-entropy by 5.47 pp on the mean, and by 8.87 in MF.
The MLP on the raw profile wins at 44.51; the best one-dimensional CNN reaches only 41.16.
Vision backbones score 36.99 to 37.62, so topology alone clears the naive baseline by only 0.95 pp.
transition: Now the second generation, starting with fixed propagation and the vector head.

title: One or two hops, high retention
points: The best depth is one step in BP, two in CC, and zero in MF.
Beyond the peak, performance falls by 12.80 to 17.60 pp by T equal to 10.
Retention peaks at 0.7 in BP and 0.8 in CC; low retention is clearly worse.
The graph works as a correction to the protein's own representation, not a replacement.
transition: The vision head behaves differently.

title: The vision head wants deep propagation
points: The vision head peaks at seven steps in BP and six in CC, more a plateau than a peak.
It gains 5.84 pp in BP and 2.93 in CC from propagation, against 1.85 and 0.92 for the vector head.
It collapses at α of 0.2 or lower, because isolated nodes are scaled by α to the power T.
Its best BP value, 52.17, is still below the vector head without any graph, at 53.36.
transition: Next, fixed against learned aggregation.

title: Learning the aggregation does not pay
points: The GCN beats the GAT in all six pairs, by 3.88 to 9.31 pp, and in all 30 fusion pairs.
The fixed operator averages 65.12, against 63.32 for the GCN.
The GCN leads in BP by 0.55, a tie, and trails by 0.59 in CC and 5.35 in MF.
Every deduplication difference beyond the noise favours the maximum rule, up to 3.83 pp for the GAT.
transition: Then, fusion.

title: Fusion helps; combining predictions helps more
points: Early fusion's best configuration reaches 65.80, 0.68 above the fixed route alone.
Late fusion wins: a linear mix with γ at 0.50 in BP and 0.55 in CC and MF reaches 67.06.
It gains 2.18 pp in BP, 1.85 in CC and 1.26 in MF over its better component, with one extra fitted parameter.
Stacking models put almost all weight on the two probabilities, not on information content or degree.
transition: Across all stages, which head is better?

title: Vector head wins 12 of 12
points: The vector head beats the vision head in all twelve comparisons.
The mean margin is 6.62 pp in the first generation, 3.96 with fixed propagation, 2.69 with the GNN and 3.35 with early fusion.
It narrows, but shows no trend toward zero.
Neither image has the locality a convolution assumes.
transition: This next chart summarizes the whole validation journey.

title: Where the gains come from
points: The naive baseline sits at 43.56 and the first generation at 44.51, less than one point apart.
ProtT5 alone, with the graph off, jumps to 63.92.
Fixed propagation reaches 65.12, early fusion 65.84 and late fusion 67.06.
Most of the jump comes from the language model; the graph adds a consistent remainder, mainly in BP and CC.
transition: Now the test set, read once, against five methods from the literature.

title: Test set: NEXUS-GO vs five methods
points: NEXUS-GO/Late has the best value in every test column across six metrics, except AuPRC in MF.
Its margin over DeepGraphGO is 9.77 pp in BP, 8.67 in CC and 4.93 in MF.
S_min agrees: 17.12 against 20.11 bits in BP, 8.22 against 9.67 in CC, 5.14 against 5.67 in MF.
The ProtT5 baseline alone already beats every literature method on wF_max.
All baselines were retrained on the same corpus, so this ordering describes the adapted configurations.
transition: Coverage puts these margins in perspective.

title: Every protein gets a prediction
points: Every NEXUS-GO route predicts 100% of the test partition.
DeepGraphGO and SEGT-GO reach 95.1 to 96.3% using a homology search.
Mashup, MELISSA and deepNF only see network members, covering 63.6 to 68.7%.
Part of the distance to network-only methods is reach, not ranking quality.
transition: What does each route cost?

title: A thirteenth of the time per epoch
points: Fixed propagation with the vector head trains at 5.24 seconds per epoch with 6.4 GiB of peak memory.
The GCN takes 68.76 seconds and 14.1 GiB, and the GAT 161.41 seconds and 20.7 GiB.
The fixed operator matches or beats the GCN at about a thirteenth of the time per epoch.
The reason is structural: the fixed operator runs once, the learned one at every step.
transition: Finally, where does the graph help?

title: The graph helps where there is graph
points: Every ProtT5 route scores worse on connected proteins than on isolated ones, and the graph-free control shows it too.
Hubs tend to be multifunctional and harder for a sequence model.
The gain over the control grows with degree, up to 9.05 pp in BP, 8.71 in CC and 4.64 in MF.
The graph helps where there is graph.
transition: Part six: the conclusions, starting with the answers.

title: Answers to the research questions
points: The best network representation is the unreduced profile with an MLP; imposing locality hurts.
Most of the gain comes from ProtT5; on test, propagation adds 1.87 pp in BP, 2.15 in CC and nothing in MF.
Late fusion leads at 67.06 on validation and helps by 1.26 to 2.18 pp; one or two hops with α of 0.7 to 0.8 work best.
NEXUS-GO/Late beats the literature by 9.77, 8.67 and 4.93 pp of wF_max, on one global aggregated network.
transition: These results come with limitations.

title: Limitations
points: All runs use a single seed, so the 0.5 pp floor is a reading convention, not a confidence interval.
The random protein-level split measures transductive interpolation, and some homology is possible.
STRING scores include curated databases and text mining, which may leak functional knowledge.
Fixed versus learned is not a single-factor ablation, and the baselines were adapted to our setting.
transition: These limitations point to the next steps.

title: Next steps
points: Separate the graph by organism, or train one model per organism.
Keep STRING evidence channels apart, so experimental evidence counts differently from text mining.
Try heterogeneous graphs, compared with methods such as ProtHGT, and sampled aggregation as in GraphSAGE.
Richer node features are most promising for MF, where the network contributed the least.
transition: Let me conclude.

title: Thank you
points: NEXUS-GO propagates ProtT5 over STRING with a fixed operator and matches a learned encoder at a fraction of its cost.
Its fusion with a GCN is the best evaluated method in every ontology.
The code is public on GitHub, with a VISAPP 2026 paper and an extended version accepted in CCIS.
I thank the committee, my advisors, CAPES, BTG Pactual and the Institute of Computing.
transition: Thank you very much; I am happy to take your questions.
